title: Early-detect noisy tenant & soft-resize playbook for dedicated clusters
creator: Asha Mehta
description:
Summary:
This ticket captures a pragmatic playbook and follow-ups from recent dedicated-cluster capacity incidents where tenant-level mis-sizing and aggressive burst windows caused noisy-neighbor effects and elevated eviction rates. The goal is to reduce detection time, automate a conservative soft-resize response, and provide operational runbooks that avoid broad evictions or customer-visible tail latency spikes.

Problem statement:
- We observed tenants with intermittent heavy micro-bursts that saturated per-GPU shared resources (KV cache pressure, CUDA memory contention) causing eviction cascades and tail latencies for colocated tenants.
- Existing alarms are aggregate (node-level) and trigger late after evictions are already in motion. Reservation sizing is static and lacks a staged soft-degradation option before full eviction. Burst token-buckets allow large one-shot bursts that destabilize packing.

Goals / success metrics:
- Detect noisy-tenant behavior within 90s of onset using tenant-level signals.
- Automate a non-disruptive soft-resize within 120s for >80% of noisy events, reducing downstream eviction incidence by 60% in canary clusters.
- Add a playbook and console links so SRE can respond within 5 minutes for manually escalated incidents.

Scope & constraints:
- Applies to Dedicated GPU pools and dedicated-tenant scheduling path only. Does not change customer-visible reservation contracts; soft-resize must be conservative and reversible.
- Must be robust to telemetry delays (up to 30s).

Detection heuristics (draft):
- Primary signals (tenant-level, sliding window 60s):
  * Sustained token consumption > 3x tenant historical median RPS or > 95th percentile of that tenant for 60s.
  * KV cache miss rate spike > 30% relative within 60s paired with per-GPU mem alloc churn > 25MB/s.
  * P90 tail latency increase > 4x baseline for internally observed inference pipelines.
- Secondary signals (corroboration):
  * Node-level OOM/kern logs correlate with tenant's CUDA PIDs within 120s.
  * Inter-tenant latency correlation where >2 neighbors show latency uplift within same node.
- Trigger rule: primary signal + one secondary OR primary signal sustained for 90s.

Soft-resize response (automated staged actions):
1) Stage 0 (informational): annotate tenant in console (no change) and fire an incident channel.
2) Stage 1 (conservative throttle, 0-30s after trigger): apply short-lived token-bucket limit reduction of 20% for tenant; enable prefix KV caching if request patterns match.
3) Stage 2 (soft-resize, 30-120s): temporarily scale reservation down by up to 30% or move the tenant to a lower QoS lane for new requests only; keep existing KV cache warm for in-flight contexts.
4) Stage 3 (isolate, manual-only): when automated steps do not reduce node pressure within 3 minutes, mark tenant for manual sandboxing and schedule migration off overloaded node.

Rationale for staged approach:
- Avoid hard evictions which invalidate KV caches and increase downstream work.
- Soft-resize focuses on new request admission control and modestly reducing working set to alleviate cache pressure.
- Conservative caps preserve SLA promises while stopping cascades.

Telemetry & queries to adopt (initial):
- Tenant token burn rate: sum(tokens) by tenant over 30s and 60s windows.
- KV cache pressure: evictions/sec and cache hit ratio by tenant.
- Per-GPU resident memory drift and allocation churn by pid/tenant.
- Inter-tenant latency cross-correlation matrix per node.
Instrumentation tasks:
- Add tenant-id tagging to GPU allocator metrics (ENG infra change) - small agent bump.
- Expose token-bucket state and TTLs to console for fast debugging.
- Build a Grafana dashboard with the detection rule and annotations for automated actions.

Testing & canary rollout plan:
- Unit tests for detection rule and simulated noisy tenancy in local test harness.
- Staging run: enable detection + Stage 1 actions in a staging dedicated cluster for 2 weeks and gather metrics on false positives/negatives.
- Canary: enable full staged automation in 2 small production pools (low risk customers) for 7 days, then expand.

Operational runbook (SRE steps):
- On alert: check the tenant dashboard link, confirm primary + secondary signals.
- If Stage1 already applied and node stabilized: close incident, annotate root cause.
- If Stage2 applied: monitor KV hit ratio and tail latency; if no improvement within 3 minutes, escalate to manual isolation.
- Post-incident: tag ticket with causal classification (mis-sizing|spike pattern|software regression).

Open technical tasks (action items):
- T1: Implement detection rule and alert (owner: Martin Gomez). Acceptance: alerts within 90s of simulated noisy injection. (estimate 3)
- T2: Implement soft-resize API and token-bucket throttle controller (owner: Priya Rao). Acceptance: staged actions can be triggered by detection rule in staging. (estimate 5)
- T3: Add tenant tags to GPU allocator and KV cache metrics (owner: Infra team — Liaison: Daniel Park). Acceptance: allocator metrics include tenant_id label. (estimate 3)
- T4: Build dashboard and incident playbook doc (owner: oncall docs — author: Asha Mehta). Acceptance: runbook published and linked in alert. (estimate 2)
- T5: Conduct canary and adjust thresholds based on false-positive rate (owner: SRE rotation). Acceptance: FP rate < 5% after 2 weeks. (estimate 3)

Acceptance criteria for this ticket:
- Detection + Stage1 automation merged and running in staging with recorded test runs.
- Playbook doc (this runbook) published and linked in Console incident page.
- Postmortem action items assigned and scheduled.

Notes / risks:
- Risk of over-throttling a bursty but legitimate tenant; mitigated by conservative initial limits and automatic rollback if downstream KPIs improve.
- Telemetry tagging touches low-level allocator code; may require coordination with device driver team for releases.

Related artifacts:
- Mock dashboards and query notes in attachments.
- PR placeholders and RFC notes below.
